chapters.title: The World of the Greek Gods

pages.text: The ancient Greeks explained the world through stories about gods. These gods were not distant, silent powers. They were passionate, jealous, generous, petty, and occasionally foolish beings who took an active and often unhelpful interest in human affairs. They lived on Mount Olympus, the highest mountain in Greece, and from there they watched, argued, and intervened in the lives of humans for reasons that were sometimes just and sometimes entirely personal.

image.note: Illustration: Mount Olympus above the clouds, divine figures visible at its peak

pages.text: The twelve Olympians were: Zeus, king of the gods and ruler of the sky; Hera, his wife and queen; Poseidon, god of the sea; Demeter, goddess of the harvest; Athena, goddess of wisdom; Apollo, god of the sun and music; Artemis, goddess of the hunt; Ares, god of war; Aphrodite, goddess of love; Hephaestus, god of the forge; Hermes, messenger of the gods; and Dionysus, god of wine. Below the Olympians were hundreds of lesser gods, nymphs, spirits, and demigods.

The Greek myths were not simply entertainment. They explained natural phenomena: why there are seasons, why the sun moves across the sky, why there is death in the world. They provided models of heroic behaviour and cautionary examples of what happened to those who were proud, greedy, or foolish enough to challenge the gods. They remain some of the most enduring stories ever told.

Demeter, goddess of the harvest, had a daughter called Persephone, whom she loved above all things. One day, while Persephone was picking flowers in a meadow, the earth opened and Hades, king of the underworld, pulled her down into his realm and made her his queen.

image.note: Illustration: Persephone in a sunlit meadow, flowers around her, a dark chasm opening at her feet

pages.text: Demeter searched the earth for her daughter, abandoning her duties. The crops died. The earth grew cold. People began to starve. Zeus, alarmed, sent Hermes to the underworld to retrieve Persephone. But Hades had given her pomegranate seeds to eat, knowing that anyone who ate food in the underworld was bound to return. Persephone had eaten six seeds.

A compromise was reached. Persephone would spend six months each year with Hades in the underworld, and six months above the earth with her mother. While Persephone is below, Demeter grieves, and the earth is cold and bare. When Persephone returns, Demeter rejoices, and the earth flowers again. This is why there are seasons.

The Greeks had a story for how the world itself began. In the beginning there was only Chaos, a vast emptiness, and from it came Gaia, the earth, and Uranus, the sky. Their children were the Titans, giant elder gods, and the youngest and boldest of them, Cronus, overthrew his own father to rule. But Cronus feared the same fate from his children, and so he swallowed each one at birth, until his wife hid the youngest away.

That youngest child was Zeus. Raised in secret, he grew strong, freed his swallowed brothers and sisters, and led them in a tremendous war against the Titans that shook the world. When it was won, Zeus and his siblings took their thrones on Mount Olympus, and the age of the Olympian gods began. Every Greek myth unfolds in the shadow of that struggle: a family of gods who gained their power by overthrowing the generation before, and who never quite trust one another.

Daedalus was the greatest craftsman and inventor in the ancient world. He built the labyrinth for King Minos of Crete to contain the Minotaur, a creature with the head of a bull and the body of a man. Having built it, Daedalus was imprisoned so that he could not reveal its secrets.

image.note: Illustration: Daedalus attaching feathered wings to his son Icarus with wax

pages.text: Daedalus made two pairs of wings from feathers and wax, one for himself and one for his son Icarus. 'Do not fly too low,' he warned. 'The sea spray will weigh the feathers down. And do not fly too high. The sun will melt the wax.' Icarus nodded. They flew. Icarus, feeling the joy of flight for the first time, climbed higher and higher. The wax melted. The feathers came apart. Icarus fell into the sea.
Daedalus reached Sicily safely. He spent the rest of his life building extraordinary things. He never flew again.
Moral: Ignore good advice at your peril. Joy is not an excuse for recklessness.

Orpheus was a musician of such extraordinary skill that his music could charm animals, make rivers stop flowing, and move stones to tears. When his wife Eurydice died from a snakebite, Orpheus descended into the underworld to bring her back.

image.note: Illustration: Orpheus playing his lyre before Hades and Persephone, shades of the dead listening

pages.text: Hades, who had never been moved by anything, was moved by Orpheus's music. He agreed: Orpheus could lead Eurydice back to the world of the living, but she must follow behind him, and he must not look back at her until they had both reached the sunlight. Orpheus agreed. They climbed. Orpheus could hear nothing behind him. He began to doubt. Was she there? As they approached the surface, his doubt overwhelmed him. He looked back. Eurydice, who was only a step behind, faded back into shadow.
There are things in the world that can only be had if you do not clutch at them. Orpheus understood too late.

In the beginning, humans had no fire. They were cold, they ate raw food, and they lived at the mercy of every predator and every winter. The gods saw this and were largely unmoved. But Prometheus, a Titan, felt differently.

image.note: Illustration: Prometheus on a cliff edge, a torch of fire in his hand, Mount Olympus behind him, dark earth below

pages.text: Prometheus stole fire from the hearth of the gods and gave it to humans. With fire, humans could warm their homes, cook their food, make tools from metal, and build the first civilisations. Zeus was furious. He chained Prometheus to a rock and sent an eagle each day to eat his liver, which regrew each night. Prometheus suffered this punishment for centuries, until Hercules eventually freed him.
Prometheus knew what Zeus's punishment would be. He gave humanity fire anyway. The story of Prometheus is the story of what it costs to give people what they need to be free.

One hero towers above the rest: Heracles, whom the Romans called Hercules. Born to a mortal woman and to Zeus himself, he was hated by the goddess Hera and driven, as punishment for a terrible act committed in madness, to perform twelve seemingly impossible labours. He strangled a lion no weapon could pierce. He killed the many-headed hydra, which grew two heads for each one cut off, by burning each stump. He cleaned in a day stables that had not been cleaned in thirty years.

The labours of Heracles are the Greek idea of heroism laid bare: not that a hero never suffers, but that a hero endures. He is stronger than any man, yet the gods make his life harder than any man's. He completes his tasks not because they are fair but because giving up is unthinkable. When at last he dies and is carried up to Olympus to live among the gods, it is presented as something earned. To the Greeks, greatness was measured not in ease but in what a person could bear.
